key: Three places of the Asvins, erst concealed, are made apparent now.
s: Closing a long summons of the Asvins to the Kanvas’ Soma, the hymn turns to their approach; Sāyaṇa, on 8.8.23, takes the three places as the three wheels of their chariot, hidden until now, citing another hymn for its three wheels.

evidence.words: त्रीणि त्रिसंख्याकानि अनयोः “अश्विनोः देवयो रथस्य संबन्धीनि “पदानि चक्राणि “गुहा गुहायां वर्तमानान्येतावन्तं कालमदृश्यमानानि “परः गुहायाः परस्ताद्दृष्टिगोचरे देशे “आविः “सन्ति आविर्भवन्ति ॥ सांहितिकश्छन्दसो दीर्घः। व्यत्ययेन निघाताभावः । यद्वा । सन्तीत्येतत् अस्तेः शतरि जसि रूपम् ।। आविर्भूतानि दृश्यन्ते । आश्विनस्य रथस्य चक्रत्रयोपेतत्वं च रथस्त्रिचक्रः परि वर्तते ' (ऋ. सं. ४. ३६. १ ) इत्यादिनिगमान्तरे प्रसिद्धम् ।
evidence.gloss: The three padas of the chariot of these two gods, the Aśvins, are its wheels: lying in a hiding place and unseen until this time, they now become manifest beyond the hiding place, in a region within sight. (Grammatical notes.) They are seen made manifest. That the Aśvins’ chariot has three wheels is well known from another Vedic text, such as ‘the three-wheeled chariot goes round’ (Rig Veda 4.36.1).

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Rig Veda 8.8.23 at [627,23]). The packet’s Sanskrit (trīṇi padāny aśvinor āviḥ santi guhā paraḥ) is the app’s 8.8.23, the last verse of the hymn. Sāyaṇa takes the three padas as the wheels of the Aśvins’ chariot, hidden and unseen until now, now manifest, and supports the three wheels from another text, RV 4.36.1 (nigamāntare prasiddham); Wilson (vol. 4, packet) follows: ‘The three wheels (of the chariot) of the Aśvins, which were invisible, have become manifest’. Plain sense faithful: 8.8 summons the Asvins to the Kanvas’ Soma (3, 4), and the verse’s second half calls them hither; it closes the hymn. Revision 208919 dated 2019-08-07 by the Wikisource API.
